extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, editors, journalism students, and media/ethics scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for ethical practices in photojournalism, especially concerning image manipulation, publication decisions, privacy, and the challenges posed by digital and citizen photography. Includes institutional codes (e.g., NYT, NPPA) and case-study examples (Walski, Abu Ghraib, Snelgrove).

rubrics_metrics.name: Images must be genuine in every way (The New York Times guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Images in our pages that purport to depict reality must be genuine in every way. No people or objects may be added, rearranged, reversed, distorted or removed from a scene (except for the recognized practice of cropping to omit extraneous outer portions). Adjustments of color or gray scale should be limited to those minimally necessary for clear and accurate reproduction, analogous to the 'burning' and 'dodging' that formerly took place in darkroom processing of images. Pictures of news situations must not be posed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collages, montages, portraits, fashion or home design illustrations, fanciful contrived situations and demonstrations of how a device is used should have intervention unmistakable to the reader and free of intent to deceive. Captions and credits should further acknowledge intervention if the slightest doubt is possible. Consult the design director, a masthead editor or the news desk on doubtful cases or proposals for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain integrity of photographic content and context (NPPA code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing should maintain the integrity of the photographic images' content and context. Do not manipulate images in any way that can mislead viewers or misrepresent subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPPA code (and its digital amendment) is presented as the closest thing to a unified standard; violations can lead to membership review and possible expulsion. The Walski incident is used as an example of manipulation that misrepresented interaction between subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not manipulate key elements of a news photograph
rubrics_metrics.description: Key elements of a news photograph, like the key words in a direct quote, are off limits to manipulation. Any manipulation that changes who is in the frame, their actions, or the apparent interaction between subjects is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous admonition: 'If you can't do it in the darkroom, don't do it here.' Walski's composite (combining two frames to make subjects appear to interact) violated this principle even though each source image was similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label and disclose interventions (photo-illustrations / collages)
rubrics_metrics.description: When images are collages, montages, or otherwise contrived or demonstrative, the intervention should be unmistakable to the reader and captions/credits should acknowledge the intervention if any doubt exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even skillful manipulations can be ethically acceptable if clearly labeled (e.g., 'composographs' historically were labeled). Publications insist on labeling ex post facto manipulations as 'photo-illustrations' to avoid deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crop and tonal adjustments limited to minimal, clarifying edits
rubrics_metrics.description: Cropping is permitted to omit extraneous outer portions; adjustments of color or gray scale should be limited to those minimally necessary for clear and accurate reproduction, analogous to traditional darkroom burning and dodging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modest adjustments are distinguished from manipulations that alter content or context. NYT guidance and industry practice accept cropping and small tonal fixes but not changes that mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not stage or pose news situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures of news situations must not be posed; photojournalists should avoid recreating or staging events for the sake of a better image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staging undermines the role of the photographer as a documenter of what happened. The NYT guideline and other professional commentary emphasize non-intervention in news scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographer vs editor responsibilities (capture vs publish)
rubrics_metrics.description: The photographer's duty is to capture the event; the editor's duty is to decide whether to publish. Field photographers should not preemptively withhold images solely because they feel uneasy—editing/publishing decisions belong to editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues it's almost impossible to make complex ethical publication decisions in real time; better to photograph and allow the editor to judge later. If an image is too graphic or intrusive, the editor can choose not to run it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh newsworthiness against taste and potential harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must consider whether publishing an image is worth embarrassing the subject, whether the image is too graphic or in poor taste, and whether its public interest outweighs possible harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abu Ghraib photos provided an example where newsworthiness and public accountability outweighed concerns about taste and the fact images were not taken by professionals. Editors balanced shock value against the images' role in exposing abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy standard—reasonable expectation of privacy dictates actionability
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject of the photograph has no reasonable expectation of privacy, then no invasion of privacy is possible; photographs taken in public places generally are not actionable. Photos of crimes, arrests and accidents are usually considered newsworthy and immune from privacy claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/privacy guidance (Reporters’ Committee for a Free Press) is used to argue that photographing Snelgrove on a public street was not legally prohibited, though some saw it as poor taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting and verifying citizen-submitted images
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms must be cautious when using images taken by the general public—verify authenticity before publication because amateurs may be unaware of ethical nuances or may intentionally produce fakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fake Kerry–Fonda composite and a hoax iPod photo demonstrate potential real-world consequences (election misinformation, stock-market impact). Editors inundated with public submissions may lack time to fully vet images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of technology-driven ethical changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital photography, powerful editing software, ubiquitous camera-equipped mobile devices, and new in-camera features have drastically changed the ethical landscape by making manipulation easier and by increasing the volume and immediacy of images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, film/darkroom constraints limited manipulation. Software like Adobe Photoshop and features like in-camera multiple exposure (Nikon D2x) change what is possible and what must be ethically regulated; ethical standards sometimes lag behind technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish professional standards from nonprofessional/citizen work
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionalism involves technical skill, news-gathering experience, and adherence to a code of ethics; citizen images may lack these and can be misused or misinterpreted without proper context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite ubiquity of cameras, professionals provide judgment, verification, and ethical discipline. The New York Times ran a citizen camera-phone image, but running a citizen-written news piece on the front page would be unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid decontextualization and contextual misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: An image's meaning can be manipulated through use in a false context or no context at all; editors must guard against publishing photos that misleadingly change the perceived reality of an event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peter Howe's example: the same photograph of soldiers with money could be interpreted in multiple ways depending on context—responsible use requires appropriate context to avoid misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and accountability for ethical breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional organizations (e.g., NPPA) have bylaws describing recourse for members who violate codes of ethics, including judiciary review and potential revocation of membership; employers may impose further consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While organizational sanctions exist, membership is not required for industry work, so consequences vary; public and editorial reaction (firings, apologies) are also forms of accountability illustrated by Walski and other cases.
